value.overview: The Bronzy Hermit (Glaucis aeneus) is a small hummingbird of humid lowlands in Central America and northwestern South America. It belongs to the hermit hummingbird group, whose members often have long, curved bills and forage in shaded vegetation. The species is associated with Heliconia thickets, forest edges, swampy ground, streams, and regenerating forest. Costa Rica is an important part of its Central American range and is also the species’ type locality.
value.classification: The Bronzy Hermit is a hummingbird in the family Trochilidae and the hermit subfamily Phaethornithinae. It is the only recognized species in its genus occurring in Costa Rica and is closely related to the Rufous-breasted Hermit.
value.identification: This is a small, long-billed hermit, about 8–10 cm long. It has bronzy or coppery-green upperparts, a dusky face with a pale moustache-like marking, a warm buff throat and breast, and a paler belly. The bill is long and strongly downcurved, usually dark above and paler below. The tail appears gray-green or bronzy from above, with contrasting pale tips and darker central areas. Sexes are similar in appearance.
value.rangeHabitat: The Bronzy Hermit occurs from eastern Honduras through Nicaragua and Costa Rica to western Panama, with a separate population in western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a lowland and lower-foothill resident, recorded on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, generally from sea level to about 750 m. It favors humid forest edges, disturbed primary forest, mature secondary growth, swamp forest, streamside thickets, and dense stands of Heliconia, often using semi-open, tangled vegetation rather than deep forest interior.
value.migrationStatus: Resident and generally non-migratory. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round in suitable lowland and foothill habitats; regular long-distance seasonal migration is not known.
value.breeding: The breeding season is not completely documented across the species’ range. In Costa Rica, nesting may occur during much of the wetter part of the year, with timing varying by region and elevation. The female builds a small cone-shaped cup from plant fibers and spider web, often adding lichens for camouflage. The nest is attached beneath the tip or underside of a drooping leaf. The usual clutch is two eggs, and the female handles most incubation and care of the young.
value.dietFeeding: The Bronzy Hermit feeds mainly on nectar from long, tubular flowers, especially Heliconia and related plants. Its long, curved bill is well suited to probing these flowers. It also takes small arthropods, including spiders and insects. Such prey may be gleaned from leaves, twigs, and spider webs or occasionally caught in flight. It commonly forages in shaded thickets, forest edges, streamside vegetation, and other dense lowland growth.
value.behavior: Like other hermits, the Bronzy Hermit often moves quietly through dense vegetation and may be easier to detect by its sharp calls or rapid wingbeats than by sight. It commonly perches low in thickets and makes short feeding flights between flowers. Individuals usually forage alone and defend favored feeding areas, although several may use a productive flowering patch. Its song consists of high, thin notes delivered in descending or irregular phrases.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size and population trend have not been reliably quantified.
